details: Primary legal framework: Ukraine Law 'On the Legal Status of the Territory That Suffered from the Chernobyl Catastrophe' (December 28 1991 No. 796-XII); established: (1) Zone of Alienation (30km zone; access prohibited without permit); (2) Zone of Unconditional Resettlement (contamination >555 kBq/m²); (3) Zone of Guaranteed Voluntary Resettlement (185-555 kBq/m²); (4) Zone of Enhanced Ecological Control (37-185 kBq/m²); zones based on Cs-137 contamination level; Cabinet of Ministers establishes specific boundaries
current_status: Law 796 framework still in force 2026; modified by subsequent resolutions; SNRIU has regulatory authority for radiation aspects; Ministry of Ecology has environmental authority; Chernobyl NPP (State Specialized Enterprise SSE CHNPP) manages site operations; 2022 Russian occupation: SSE CHNPP staff maintained skeleton presence through occupation period March-April 2022; functions resumed after Russian withdrawal March 31 2022
source: Ukraine Law No. 796-XII 1991; SNRIU regulatory authority; chernobyl_unit_operations_REAL.csv

details: Chernobyl Exclusion Zone (Zone of Alienation): approximately 2600 km² centered on ChNPP; irregular shape reflecting contamination pattern rather than perfect circle; extends further in NW direction (highest contamination plume); 30km nominal but boundary adjusted to follow contamination contours; within CEZ: Chernobyl town (partially accessible with permits); Pripyat (access with permits); NPP site; Red Forest; 7 km² inner security zone around NPP (higher security)
current_status: CEZ access control: checkpoints at CEZ boundary; entry requires: permit from SNRIU; dosimetric equipment; authorized guide/escort; radiation protection training; temporary access: scientific research; decommissioning work; nuclear tourism (suspended 2022; some resumed 2023 for day trips); agricultural use prohibited; wild game hunting prohibited (radiation levels in meat); wood harvesting restricted

details: CEZ radiation monitoring infrastructure: (1) SNRIU environmental monitoring stations: >30 permanent stations in CEZ; gamma dose rate H*(10); automatic data transmission; public access via SNRIU website; (2) SaveEcoBot network: commercial monitoring stations with public API; real-time dose rate at CEZ sites and across Ukraine; (3) EURDEP: Ukrainian monitoring data integrated into European network; (4) ChNPP site-specific: NSC sensors (5000+); ISF monitoring; spent fuel storage monitoring; (5) Air monitoring: filters at multiple CEZ locations for alpha/beta aerosol
current_status: Monitoring continuity during 2022 occupation: SNRIU lost access to Zaporizhzhia Oblast monitoring; ~40% Ukrainian monitoring network in occupied/front-line territory; ChNPP monitoring maintained (SSE CHNPP staff + IAEA on-site); Oct 2025 power loss: 16hr backup power used for monitoring continuity; SaveEcoBot provided real-time data to public throughout war period; current (April 2026): monitoring coverage partial due to war

details: Scientific research in CEZ: procedure (pre-war): (1) submit proposal to SSE CHNPP and SNRIU; (2) risk assessment; (3) radiation protection plan; (4) approval typically 2-4 weeks; (5) mandatory dosimetric monitoring during field work; (6) field TLD + alarm dosimeter; (7) decontamination on exit; (8) dose record; types of research: environmental monitoring; wildlife biology; radioecology; archaeology; materials science; NSC structural monitoring; International research: STAR (Strategy for Allied Radioecology) consortium; various EU-funded projects
current_status: Major ongoing research programs (2026): (1) Beresford 2022 STAR radioecology (44 taxa dose assessment); (2) IAEA MODAS (CEZ dose assessment model); (3) wildfire monitoring (Evangeliou group; NorESM model); (4) Am-241 ingrowth measurement (cross-validates Bateman equations in am241_ingrowth_timeseries_REAL.csv); (5) Frog melanin evolution (Burraco group); (6) CEZ cultural heritage; 2022-2025: many international research programs interrupted; Ukrainian scientists continued with reduced capacity

details: Agricultural prohibition in CEZ: all crop production prohibited within Zone of Alienation since 1986; livestock farming prohibited; wild game: hunting technically prohibited but some illegal hunting; wild berries and mushrooms: technically prohibited for collection but difficult to enforce; practical situation: some self-settlers grow garden vegetables; consume mushrooms and berries; self-settler diet monitoring shows Cs-137 body burdens consistent with consumption of local produce
current_status: Wild mushroom/berry collection in restricted zones: significant ongoing exposure pathway even with prohibition; enforcement limited; forest roads accessible to local population; Cs-137 in forest mushrooms can exceed 100,000 Bq/kg dry weight; self-settlers accepting this risk; see cez_ecosystem_ecology_REAL.csv and cs137_body_burden_ukraine_REAL.csv for pathway data; Prussian Blue animal fodder available but not always used

details: Experimental CEZ agriculture (IAEA partnership 2019-present): 100 hectares of formerly abandoned farmland within Zone of Guaranteed Voluntary Resettlement (outer CEZ); trials of: sunflowers for biodiesel; energy crops; phytoremediation species; objective: demonstrate productive use of contaminated land; crop Cs-137 monitored; sunflowers for oil (NOT food): Cs-137 in oil negligible (does not partition to oil fraction); biomass crops: Cs-137 stays in structural components (stems) not exported if roots not included; successful in demonstrating non-food productive use
current_status: IAEA agricultural trial demonstrates: abandoned land can be productively used for non-food applications even without full decontamination; reduces stigma of contaminated land; provides economic activity for resettlement areas; however: any food production would require extensive monitoring; staple crops (wheat, potato) remain prohibited; Ukrainian government exploring expanded use of outer CEZ zones; see cez_research_2022_2025_REAL.csv

details: CEZ waste management activities (2026): (1) ISF-2 fuel loading: continuing transfer from ISF-1 wet pool; target completion 2028; (2) Solid Radioactive Waste treatment facility: processing legacy waste from decontamination; (3) Red Forest stabilization: monitoring burial trench migration; groundwater monitoring around sites; (4) Liquid waste treatment: continued processing of radioactive water accumulated in basement of Shelter; (5) Equipment decontamination at Rossokha vehicle graveyard: vehicles being sorted for burial vs decontamination
current_status: 2022 disruption: ISF-2 loading paused during Russian occupation; waste treatment reduced; groundwater monitoring maintained by skeleton staff; March 2022 Russian forces dug trenches through Red Forest (near waste burial sites); IAEA inspection post-March 2022 found no significant additional contamination from trench digging activity; waste management programs re-accelerated April 2022 onwards with international support

details: UNESCO World Heritage nomination: Ukraine submitted Chernobyl nomination dossier for UNESCO World Heritage status; nomination being considered 2022+; category: cultural landscape; sites: Chernobyl NPP (sarcophagus/NSC); Pripyat ghost city; memorial complex; CEZ as nature reserve; arguments for: unique cultural/historical significance; testimony to nuclear age; exceptional nature recovery; arguments against: active industrial site (decommissioning ongoing); radiation hazard; war conditions 2022+
current_status: UNESCO WH consideration postponed due to war 2022+; Pripyat: most photographed ghost city globally; represents unique intersection of: nuclear age technology; Soviet history; forced abandonment; ecological recovery; architectural history; preserved under radiation protection regime; if designated: formal preservation program; controlled tourism; heritage management; NSC drone strike 2025 adds urgency to heritage protection

details: Radiation dose limits for CEZ workers: Ukrainian occupational limit = ICRP 103 recommendation = 20 mSv/year effective dose (averaged over 5 years; max 50 mSv in any single year); eye lens: 20 mSv/year (ICRP 118 revised); skin: 500 mSv/year; hands/feet: 500 mSv/year; for ChNPP decommissioning workers: same 20 mSv/year; liquidators 1986 nominal limit: 25 rem/year = 250 mSv/year; post-Soviet Ukraine: reduced to 50 mSv → 20 mSv with EU harmonization; emergency responders: up to 100 mSv for lifesaving
current_status: SSE CHNPP workers (2026): decommissioning workers; ISF-2 loading staff; monitoring personnel; typical annual dose: 1-5 mSv/year (well below limit); some ISF workers handling higher-activity assemblies: up to 10-15 mSv/year; NSC inspection workers: <1 mSv/year; dose tracking: electronic personal dosimetry + quarterly TLD; records kept by SNRIU; EU harmonized dose limits applied since 2000
